title: Everyday repair workshop v1

training:
The repair room opens after breakfast. A small table stands near the door, and a wide shelf holds the tools. Each person brings one thing that needs attention. There is no charge to ask a question. The group tries to understand the trouble before anyone begins to work.

One morning a visitor brings a wooden chair. Its back is firm, but one leg moves when the chair is placed on the floor. The helper sets it on the table and looks at the joint. She does not pull the whole chair apart. First she marks the loose piece, then she asks the visitor to hold the other side. They clean the old glue from the wood and leave the pieces to dry.

At the next table, a man sorts screws into shallow trays. He writes the size on a card beside each tray. When someone takes a screw, he asks them to return any that do not fit. Small parts are easy to lose under a cloth or inside a deep box. Clear labels save time, but the labels must describe what is really there.

After lunch the group checks a lamp. The helper leaves it unplugged while she looks at the shade and the base. The owner says the light failed after the lamp fell from a desk. They agree that electrical work needs a qualified repairer, so they put a note on it rather than guessing. Knowing when to stop is part of doing useful work.

Before the room closes, everyone clears a place for the next group. They count the tools, wash the table, and carry the empty boxes to the back wall. A written record shows what was finished and what still needs care. The record is short enough to read, but it does not hide an unfinished job.

The chair stays in the room overnight. In the morning its owner returns and checks the joint with the helper. They place it on level ground and look for movement. If the repair is not sound, they will explain the problem instead of calling it complete. A good result is something they can check together, not just something that looks right from the door.
evaluation:
The garden shed is open on Saturday. A neighbor arrives with a hand cart and asks whether the group can inspect a wheel. The frame looks straight, but the wheel turns with a rough sound. A helper makes a note before removing anything. They set the loose parts in a tray so that nothing rolls under the bench.

Another visitor wants to mend a cloth bag. She chooses a patch from a box of clean scraps and lays it over the worn corner. The helper asks her to check the inside as well as the outside. A neat patch is not useful if the bag cannot hold its contents. They leave the handle alone because it is still strong.

At the end of the session, the neighbors write down what they have done. The cart needs another inspection, and the bag is ready to carry home. They put the tools away and leave the clear notes beside the door. Next week a different group will use the shed. Those notes should help them begin without having to guess what happened before.
